newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat appeals to Clinton to save Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: Arafat appeals to Clinton to save Mideast peace.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat urgently appealed to re-elected U.S. President Bill Clinton for a "quick push" to get Middle East peacemaking back on track.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Arabs not to expect a second-term Clinton, unfettered by the demands of an election campaign, to pressure Israel into making concessions.
Both welcomed the president's November 5 victory over Bob Dole, hailing Clinton on Wednesday as a friend of their respective peoples and a man devoted to peace.
"There must be a quick push from His Excellency (President Clinton) so that the peace process will go on the same track," Arafat told the U.S. television network CNN.

If Clinton did not act swiftly, Arafat said, "We will face some troubles and it will be a good opportunity for the extremists on the two sides -- on our side and on the Israeli side -- to sabotage more and more the peace process."
Israeli and Palestinian teams are locked in slow-moving negotiations on a long-promised Israeli handover of parts of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian self-rule.
The talks resumed on Wednesday night. Israel says it wants to boost security for the 400 Jews who live and study in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs.

Some Arabs and Israelis expect Clinton, eyeing his place in history rather than another election, will lean on Netanyahu to carry out peace deals the Israeli right-winger reluctantly inherited when he took office in June.
But Arafat said he did not expect Clinton to pressure Netanyahu.
Netanyahu, the Likud party leader, said on Tuesday he would not be "whipped" by the next president into making compromises and Arafat was wrong to think so.
U.S. Consul General Edward Abington said there were as yet no plans for Clinton's Middle East envoy Dennis Ross to return to the region to try to broker a deal.

Clinton has played a key role in the Middle East, most recently calling Arafat and Netanyahu to an emergency White House summit to stop clashes and gun battles unprecedented in three years of Israel-PLO peacemaking.

The U.S. president all but endorsed former prime minister Shimon Peres over Netanyahu in this year's Israeli election. A Nobel peace laureate, Peres favours a U.S.-backed land-for-peace policy that Netanyahu opposes.
Israeli commentators said on Wednesday the first indication of the future direction of U.S. policy would be in Clinton's appointment of a successor to retiring Secretary of State Warren Christopher.

Clinton's repeated commitment to Israel's security has many doubting he will use any of the leverage he might have against it. Israel, at $3 billion a year, receives more U.S. aid than any other country.
Finance Minister Dan Meridor said he doubted the United States would use aid to pressure Israel.

In the early 1990s then-U.S. President George Bush, angry at a Jewish settlement boom in the West Bank under the previous Likud-led government, withheld $10 billion in loan guarantees for Jewish immigrants from the former Soviet Union.
Washington awarded the loan guarantees only in 1992 when then-Labour party leader Yitzhak Rabin came to power in Israel and froze new Jewish settlement building.

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, due in Egypt on Thursday, said he hoped to hear from the Egyptians that Israel's arch-foe Syria wanted to renew peace talks stuck on the fate of the Israeli-held Golan Heights and the nature of peace.
